title: Generic constants as static final instances

blocks.text: The oldest "generic enum" pattern needs no enum at all: a generic class with `public static final` instances. Each instance carries its own type argument, even a parameterized one such as `TypedKey<List<String>>`, which a `Class` token cannot express. The price, the page says, is everything an enum gives for free: there is no `values()`, no lookup by name, and the set is closed only while the constructor stays `private`.
The starter declares the four keys and the accessors. Write the rest:

items: The constructor `TypedKey(String name, T defaultValue)` stores both and records the new key, so that `values()` can list it. No code outside the class may create a key.
`static List<TypedKey<?>> values()` lists every key in declaration order. The caller cannot change the list.
`static Optional<TypedKey<?>> named(String name)` returns the key whose `name()` equals `name`, or empty.

blocks.text: Mind the order of static initialization: a static field is initialized in the order it is written, and the constants' constructors run while the class is being initialized.

cases.says: values() lists the four keys in declaration order, each with its own typed default, and named() finds a key by name.
named() finds a key by a name built at run time, not written as the same literal.
named() of a name no key has gives an empty Optional.
The constructor is private and no public static method hands out new keys, so no code outside the class can add a key.
The list values() returns cannot be changed, so callers cannot add or remove keys through it.

concepts: A generic class with static final instances and a private constructor gives full generic typing, even for parameterized types, but has no built-in values() or lookup.
